node-1.label: Patient presented with stridor, increased work of breathing, and supplemental oxygen requirement.

node-2.label: A man presented to the emergency department on transfer from an outside hospital after falling with an e-cigarette in his mouth several hours earlier; he did not remember the exact cause of the fall but believed he may have lost consciousness.

node-3.label: Physical examination in the ED showed diffuse supraglottic edema most severe in the epiglottis, arytenoids, and aryepiglottic folds, obstructing a view of the true vocal cords.

why.why: The radiologist analysis explicitly states that CT and direct laryngoscopy findings strongly support acute supraglottic edema and that imaging and endoscopic evidence cover key diagnostic confirmation. This reinforces the physical examination and prior imaging/endoscopic evidence, so confidence is raised from 0.95 to 0.97.

The radiologist analysis, in the context of suspected e-cigarette airway injury, interprets the CT and laryngoscopy findings of supraglottic swelling and mucosal sloughing without fracture as favoring thermal/chemical injury, which supports e-cigarette airway injury as the mechanism. Confidence is raised from 0.85 to 0.9, while acknowledging that detailed e-cigarette exposure history and bronchoscopy/inflammatory markers remain unavailable.

The radiologist analysis emphasizes the absence of fracture and infectious features and states that the pattern favors thermal/chemical injury over infectious epiglottitis. This further reduces the likelihood of acute infectious epiglottitis, lowering confidence from 0.1 to 0.05.

node-7.label: CT shows glottic and supraglottic swelling without fracture

node-8.label: Direct laryngoscopy shows diffuse edema and sloughing of pharyngeal and supraglottic mucosa, most severe in epiglottis

node-9.label: Acute supraglottic edema due to e-cigarette airway injury

why.why: The radiologist analysis confirms that CT and direct laryngoscopy strongly support acute supraglottic edema and, combined with the history of falling with an e-cigarette in the mouth, favor thermal/chemical injury over infectious epiglottitis. This makes e-cigarette-associated acute supraglottic edema the leading combined explanation; confidence is raised from 0.85 to 0.9, though bronchoscopy and inflammatory markers remain unavailable.

node-10.label: Bronchoscopy and inflammatory markers remain unavailable

node-11.label: CT and direct laryngoscopy show no fracture and no infectious features
